    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren.
    • It has been revealed that daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time.
    • Recent findings suggest that kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren.

    It has been revealed that daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time. In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he presented extensive insights from his many years of research. This article explores how Kahneman’s findings, along with other insights from behavioral science, can be applied to (strategic and tactical) football analysis.

    Recent findings suggest that kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics. Together with his colleague Amos Tversky, he succeeded in combining insights from psychology with those of economics. In 2002, he became the first psychologist to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.

    According to recent reports, his research challenges the fundamental assumption that humans make rational decisions and that cognitive distortions are primarily driven by emotions. Instead, he argued that systematic thinking errors significantly influence our judgment and decision-making. These systematic errors, known as “biases,” occur in predictable ways under certain conditions.

    According to recent reports, kahneman’s work has been applied in fields such as medical diagnosis, the legal system, intelligence analysis, philosophy, statistics, and military strategy. It is therefore a logical step to apply his research to sports analysis, where strategic decisions also play a crucial role.

    “I suppose that every author has in mind a situation in which readers of their work might benefit from reading it. I imagine the coffee machine at the office, where colleagues exchange opinions and gossip. My hope is to enrich the vocabulary people use when they talk about the judgments and decisions of others (…).” – Daniel Kahneman; Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    According to recent reports, A mere list of cognitive biases is not sufficient to recognize and avoid distortions in one’s own or others’ decisions. Only through a deeper understanding of their origins and mechanisms can the vocabulary around judgment and decision-making be enriched in Kahneman’s sense. Therefore, this article sheds light on the underlying processes and mechanisms of judgment and decision errors.

    It has been revealed that we begin by examining the scientifically established dual-process model. Following that, the mechanisms of WYSIATI, substitution, and priming will be explored in the context of football. In addition, the most relevant heuristics and cognitive biases will be applied to football analysis. Finally, we will address individual factors within analysis that contribute to the emergence of bias.

    According to recent reports, this article is only the first part of a series, which will span at least three essays. The series will examine flawed judgments in football analysis and their causes within a scientific framework informed by behavioral research.

    One point should be made clear from the outset: bias (and noise) are present wherever decisions are made, and thus affect even expert judgments within their domain.

    Recent findings suggest that this article is based on a German translation of Daniel Kahneman’s work. Accordingly, the quotes cited here may not exactly match the original English wording.

    To explain human thinking, Kahneman introduces two hypothetical agents: System 1 and System 2. This model provides a framework for understanding how thought processes work. System 1 is responsible for fast thinking, it operates automatically, intuitively, and with little effort. System 2, on the other hand, governs slow thinking, it works analytically, consciously, and requires effort.

    In a recent development, these two systems interact continuously whenever we are awake. System 1 runs constantly and automatically, while System 2 operates in an energy-saving mode, only stepping in occasionally. As a result, System 2 rarely takes control. Typically, System 2 adopts the impressions and intuitions generated by System 1 and accepts its intuitive responses.

    The division of labor between the two systems is highly efficient. From an evolutionary perspective, this can be explained by the need to react swiftly to threats while also engaging in deliberate, long-term planning. Thus, the automatic System 1 developed primarily for threat detection, while the energy-intensive System 2 evolved to support complex reasoning, though it is less frequently engaged in full.

    However, it is particularly System 1 that is susceptible to cognitive biases. Due to its energy efficiency, it is limited in logic and statistical reasoning. It often tends to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. System 2, in turn, tends to adopt these flawed outputs, as it does not always monitor or correct the conclusions generated by System 1.

    The following simple and intuitive thinking task illustrates the interplay between System 1 and System 2:.

    Team A has 62% possession and wins a match 1-0. Team B has 38% possession and loses. Which team was more dominant?

    According to recent reports, of course, Team A was more dominant. At least, that’s the intuitive conclusion System 1 leads most people to. However, it neglects the fact that possession is not necessarily a reliable measure of dominance, and that match results are very imprecise indicators of performance. Despite lacking detailed data, System 1 assembles the question into a coherent picture. System 2 supports System 1’s incorrect solution, even though with minimal effort it could have reached the correct conclusion. However, System 2 is not consciously engaged.

    From this, it follows that people rely on mental shortcuts, so-called heuristics, to quickly solve complex problems. Heuristics are usually very helpful due to their efficiency but can sometimes lead to errors in judgment, known as biases. This is where the relevance for football analysis arises, as will be shown in the following section.

    “A heuristic is, technically defined, a simple procedure that helps us find adequate, though often imperfect, answers to difficult questions.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    First, I have linked a YouTube video that you should watch:.

    Recent findings suggest that even if you are already familiar with the video, its insights are remarkable. On the one hand, it can be concluded that focusing on one task can make us blind to other processes. To see and orient ourselves, we need a certain level of attention. However, the main insight of the video is that we cannot believe we have missed something so obvious. For those who did not see the gorilla, the player leaving the scene, or the curtain changing colors, it is unimaginable not to have noticed such obvious events.

    “We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Recent findings suggest that applied to our football analysis, this once again demonstrates how prone we are to errors. How can we direct our attention to all levels of football tactics when, at the slightest distraction, we don’t even see a gorilla? We are only just beginning to discover many additional dimensions of the game as reference points, alongside spatial considerations in positional play. It is not only individual situations that are overlooked due to lack of attention, but possibly entire dimensions and we may not even be aware of this.

    We only realize our mistakes when we can no longer analyze a team with the tools we have. We follow our own subjective beliefs in analysis and overlook other logical conclusions that could have been drawn equally well from the existing data. This problem becomes particularly interesting when assessing tactical risk.

    Recent findings suggest that recall the earlier question where you were asked to judge a team’s dominance based on possession percentages and the match result. System 1 constructed the best story it could from high possession and a win. What was not done, however, was likely questioning what is necessary to authentically assess a team’s dominance. We are blind to what we do not pay attention to.

    In a recent development, hasty conclusions based on limited data form the basis of many heuristics. Kahneman refers to these conclusions as “What You See Is All There Is” (WYSIATI).

    “It is easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern when you know very little.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    This central mechanism explains why consistency of information, rather than its completeness, is what primarily shapes our beliefs. Unfortunately, we also interpret information accordingly through our coherence-seeking System 1. Kahneman explains that System 1 is completely insensitive to the quality and quantity of information from which impressions and intuitions arise. System 1 looks for coherent information, while a lazy System 2 fails to check it.

    According to recent reports, “They did not want more information that might spoil their story. WYSIATI.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    To start, I have prepared a question that should first be answered:.

    How successful will Relationism be compared to Positionism in the next ten years in the top 5 leagues?

    The answer will follow at the end of this section….

    To interpret actions and processes, a complex, multidimensional understanding of the game is necessary. In analysis, we face difficult questions that can be answered on multiple levels. Often, there is not just one correct analysis, but several possibilities which together create an accurate picture.

    Sources indicate that “I know that I know nothing.” (cf. Plato, Apology 22d: “For I was conscious that I knew practically nothing…” ).

    Through reflection and the constant questioning of our observations and conclusions, we come closer to the goal of better understanding the game. The ability to accept that there are always newly introduced perspectives and interpretations fosters a deeper, more nuanced understanding. Unfortunately, when faced with complex matters, humans intuitively tend to fall into different patterns of thinking.

    Recent findings suggest that kahneman explains that even with complex questions, we rarely seem overwhelmed. We are able to provide answers to questions we do not fully understand. But why is that?

    Industry observers note that heuristics, as explained above, can be defined as mental shortcuts. Unfortunately, complex questions must also be answered in an energy-efficient way. Thus, we tend to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. This concept underlying many heuristics is called substitution. Often, we do not even notice that we have replaced a difficult question. However, we then use the answer to the simpler question to respond to the complex one. System 1 strives for the simplest possible answer to a question, while System 2, due to its inertia, does not verify the answer.

    “You are not overwhelmed, you don’t have to exert much effort, and you may not even notice that you have not answered the question that was asked of you.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    The concept of substitution is particularly pronounced when emotions are involved in the actual target question. Emotional attitudes amplify the effect. In the case of the so-called affect heuristic (judgments based on emotions), the interaction between System 1 and System 2 is especially prone to disruption. In the context of emotions and attitudes, System 2 does not act as a self-critic but rather as an advocate for the answer proposed by System 1. It looks for arguments that support its own beliefs.

    Let us return to the question posed at the beginning of this section. You most likely found an answer to how successful Relationismus will be in the future. However, instead of systematically thinking through the target question, an answer intuitively came to you that corresponds to your beliefs. The heuristic question you unconsciously answered might have been: How much do I like Guardiola’s Positionismus?

    According to recent reports, instead of searching for counterarguments against the intuitive answer, you subsequently searched for arguments that support your beliefs. To make a reliable future prediction, it would actually be necessary to free oneself from prejudices and break down the problem into its components, systematically questioning in which situations relational play is superior to positional play and in which situations the opposite is true. After all, the two philosophies can also be combined.

    It can be concluded that substitution, together with WYSIATI, forms two of the most important mechanisms in the interplay of System 1 and System 2 underlying many systematic cognitive errors. The following section will introduce another mechanism: priming.

    Recent findings suggest that priming is a fundamental mechanism that explains how we process information when thinking. Our memory plays a central role in this, more precisely, the way it connects information. This principle is called association.

    Kahneman uses a metaphor to explain association: “Like ripples on the surface of a pond, activation spreads through a small part of the vast network of associated representations.” Even a single stimulus can be enough to unconsciously activate adjacent concepts or memories.

    A priming effect occurs when a specific stimulus, a word, an image, a situation, etc. unconsciously activates certain content in memory. This automatic chain of activation influences how we think, feel, or act without us noticing. The brain essentially lays down mental pathways in the associative network, thereby facilitating the unconscious retrieval of information.

    To illustrate, here is a simple example: “If you have recently seen or heard the word eat, you will be temporarily more likely to complete the word fragment so_p as soup rather than soap. The opposite would happen if you had just seen the word wash.”– Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Priming is already being used effectively in football contexts. For example, tactical training that includes video analysis and corresponding training formats represents a form of priming. By showing (tactical) videos during team meetings or recreating game-like patterns in training sessions, players can recognize familiar situations during matches, allowing them to react more rapidly and effectively. Training decision-making under pressure and developing speed of action can therefore be linked to the priming effect.

    It has been revealed that another well-known example of this effect is the “Florida effect.” For those interested in reading more, I’ve linked the original 1996 study by John A. Bargh, Mark Chen, and Lara Burrows.

    It has been revealed that priming also plays a role in many other areas of football. It can be deliberately used to create positive outcomes, but it can also have unintended negative effects. Depending on the context, different types of priming are distinguished, such as semantic priming, affective priming, goal priming, and many more. In football, priming is also used, for example, in injury prevention and rehabilitation.

    According to recent reports, priming can also be used for the cognitive preparation of a match. In the so-called “Moments of Excellence,” players consciously recall their best past performances immediately before a game. Particularly interesting is the application of “success priming” by the coach, through the use of specific words or phrases in the pre-match talk. Attached is a 2006 study by Stajkovic, Locke, and Blair on this topic, specifically on the unconscious performance enhancement through goal activation.

    Analysts, too, are subject to unconscious priming. A glance at the final score before conducting an analysis primes their expectations and subtly shifts the approach toward explaining the outcome, even though the final score, due to its inaccuracy as a performance indicator, says little about a team’s actual dominance.

    Given the scope of the subject, an entire article could likely be written solely on the use of priming in football. In this article, however, the foundations of priming are used to understand it as one of the mechanisms underlying cognitive biases that affect football analysis.

    “They were primed to find flaws, and that is exactly what they found.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Note: An earlier version mentioned the so-called “Florida Effect.” This belongs to a group of priming phenomena that, in the context of the replication crisis, have been only weakly or not at all confirmed. Those interested in learning more can find further information in the comment section. Many thanks to “AG” for the attentive feedback!

    At the beginning of the introduction, I explained that distortions in our thinking and decision-making occur in predictable ways under certain conditions. By now, you should have developed a basic understanding of how our thinking is governed by the interaction between System 1 and System 2, how intuitive judgments arise in the process of analysis, and how mechanisms such as WYSIATI, substitution, and priming can specifically contribute to systematic biases in football analysis.

    So far, around 200 cognitive biases have been identified. However, unlike many other articles that present a long list of biases with only brief descriptions, I deliberately refrain from doing so here. In my view, a simple enumeration does little to help recognize or avoid these distortions in practice. Instead, I focus on a small number of key biases that are particularly relevant to football analysis. Part 2 of this series will examine additional biases in the context of overconfidence.

    “Coherence means that you’re going to adopt one interpretation in general. Ambiguity tends to be suppressed. This is part of the mechanism that you have here that ideas activate other ideas and the more coherent they are, the more likely they are to activate to each other. Other things that don’t fit fall by the wayside. We’re enforcing coherent interpretation. We see the world as much more coherent than it is.” – Daniel Kahneman, Edge.

    According to recent reports, what Kahneman describes here is the phenomenon called associative coherence. The processing of subjectively fitting information is facilitated by associative memory, while the processing of mismatching information is hindered. System 1 thus generates a coherent pattern of activated ideas in associative memory.

    This phenomenon inevitably leads to errors in analysis. We should be aware that our analysis alone will never capture the entirety of the subject being analyzed. The analysis is always an expression of the analyst’s beliefs and the ideas activated in their associative memory. Even though System 2 can counteract when activated, it is still influenced by System 1. The concept of associative coherence is therefore closely related to WYSIATI and priming.

    According to recent reports, as part of the outcome of associative coherence, confirmation bias can be seen. It describes our tendency to want to confirm our existing beliefs.

    “The coherence of associative activation induces a confirmatory bias when people examine a hypothesis by increasing the accessibility of hypothesis-consistent information. For example, the intention to test the proposition that ‘Sam is friendly‘ preferentially activates evidence of Sam’s friendliness, whereas testing the proposition that ‘Sam is not friendly‘ preferentially evokes instances of hostile behavior.” – Associative Processes in Intuitive Judgement.

    It has been revealed that in analysis, we tend to seek out, select, and interpret information in a way that confirms our expectations. This, of course, applies to all areas of football analysis. Active countermeasures are necessary to avoid overlooking data that contradicts one’s own hypothesis.

    To simplify the illustration of anchoring, please answer the following two questions one after the other.

    Does Cristiano Ronaldo have more or less than 1,200 international matches for the senior national team?

    How many international matches for the senior national team has Cristiano Ronaldo played?

    In a recent development, you have very likely come to the conclusion that Ronaldo has played fewer than 1,200 international matches. Nevertheless, this value probably influenced your estimate of the second question towards a number that is too high. Ronaldo has (as of March 2025) played 219 international matches.

    Sources indicate that judgments are often based on the first piece of information given, the anchor. This biases the estimate in its direction. Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two psychological mechanisms that explain this effect.

    Sources indicate that the anchoring effect is measured and demonstrated in most psychological studies using numerical estimates, for example by estimating prices or probabilities. However, such quantitative judgments are not directly present in video analysis in football. To nevertheless apply the anchoring effect to this context, a change of perspective is useful: Richards J. Heuer Jr., among others a former CIA analyst, investigated the influence of cognitive biases, including the anchoring effect, on qualitative judgment processes within the intelligence community. In his book Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, Heuer deliberately does not refer only to mere numerical estimates, but to all kinds of ongoing judgments or assessments that an analyst inherits from predecessors or gradually revises themselves. Empirical evidence for the effectiveness of anchoring effects in sports video analysis is still lacking, but an analogy via the intelligence community is plausible.

    In a recent development, as already described above, the match result provides the analyst with the first available piece of information, acting as a kind of anchor. A 4–0 or 2–1 score leads us to attribute tactical superiority to the winning team and to base our tactical assessments too strongly on the result.

    “We should, in any case, assume that every number presented to us has an anchoring effect on us (…).” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Another example of an anchoring effect in video analysis can be found when analyzing multiple matches of a team. The first game analyzed sets an initial assessment of the team’s tactical approach. As the analysis progresses, the analyst may need to revise their judgments but often fails to adjust sufficiently and remains primarily anchored to the initial assessment. This results in a biased analysis skewed toward the anchor game.

    „Even when analysts make their own initial judgment, and then attempt to revise this judgment on the basis of upcoming information or further analysis, there is much evidence to suggest that they usually do not change the judgment enough.” – Psychology of Intelligence Analysis.

    It is not surprising that people look for reference points when faced with complex challenges, the anchor provides exactly this orientation. Unfortunately, in certain cases, it distorts our decision-making. Mussweiler and Strack investigated in their study “Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect: Considering the Opposite Compensates for Selective Accessibility” how the anchoring effect can be mitigated. Simply being aware of the anchor and the effect is unfortunately not enough to avoid the bias. Instead, a strategy of deliberately thinking about the opposite proves effective in preventing it. Imagine, instead of a 4–0 victory, a 0–4 defeat, and consider how your analysis would look in that case.

    Outcome Bias describes the tendency to judge performance based on the outcome. It is closely related to the principle of anchoring. The result serves as an anchor that shifts the judgment in its direction.

    According to recent reports, unlike the example mentioned above regarding bias from the match result, Outcome Bias can be applied to all types of results. This means that individual actions and sequences by players are evaluated based on their success or failure, regardless of the actual quality of execution.

    An example of this is a successful pressing sequence that leads to winning the ball. Because of the positive outcome, the pressing is overall rated as good. However, other relevant factors, such as intensity, timing, the opponent’s reaction, etc. are either not considered at all or only insufficiently taken into account.

    If the same pressing sequence is executed again in a different game situation but fails to win the ball, the pressing is suddenly rated as poor, even though the execution was identical. This bias demonstrates how strongly the evaluation is influenced by the outcome rather than by the quality of the action itself. All actions in the game can be subject to Outcome Bias in analysis.

    To prevent Outcome Bias, the evaluation criteria should be adjusted. Instead of judging a performance by its outcome, the process quality should be assessed. This increases the likelihood of future successful actions.

    The availability heuristic describes a cognitive shortcut in which people assess the frequency or likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. In doing so, the original question: “How often does an event occur?” is replaced by a simpler one: “How easily can I recall relevant examples?”. This is a typical example of the substitution mechanism.

    According to recent reports, more vital for the availability of an action than the number of examples one can recall is how easily they come to mind, what is known as ease of retrieval. A paradoxical example illustrating the effect of the availability heuristic was demonstrated by Schwarz et al. in 1991: people are less convinced by a decision when asked to list as many arguments in favor of it as possible. This approach plays the two factors, number of arguments and ease of retrieval, against each other: the more arguments that must be generated, the harder they are to retrieve.

    In the context of football analysis, this heuristic can lead to an overestimation of certain in-game actions or patterns, particularly during live matches. Striking, prominent, or emotional moments are more easily remembered and therefore disproportionately influence our overall evaluation of the game, regardless of how frequent or relevant they actually were. The availability heuristic has a particularly strong impact on our perception of risk (explored in Part 2).

    The game scenes most readily accessible to the analyst are also heavily influenced by their subjective experiences. A wide range of impressions, such as those from previous roles, past matches, or preferred playing philosophies, shape which factors and thus which moments are emphasized in the analysis. A strong bias toward particular strategies, such as overloads in possession, can distort the analysis by neglecting other decisive elements like timing. This simply stems from the complexity and diversity inherent to football. In this way, personal experience encourages subjective conclusions through the combination of the availability heuristic and WYSIATI.

    The representativeness heuristic describes judgments about probability based on how representative something appears to be. Representativeness here refers to stereotypes and perceived similarity. When asked about probability, people often engage in substitution, evaluating plausibility instead of actual likelihood. Kahneman illustrates this with the following example:.

    “You see a person reading The Latest York Times on the New York subway. Which of the following is a better bet about the reading stranger?

    She does not have a college degree.”.

    While the more plausible story might lead you to bet on the PhD, you should consider the base rates. Given that far more people without a college degree ride the Fresh York subway than people with doctorates, the statistically sounder bet would be on the person not having a college degree. This example highlights the tension between base rate information and representativeness.

    “The representativeness heuristic is misleading when it causes people to ignore base rate information that points in a different direction.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Kahneman accordingly advises questioning the informativeness of data and anchoring probability judgments to plausible base rates. To further illustrate the relevance of this concept in a football context, consider the following recent example:.

    Recent findings suggest that at the beginning of the 2024/25 season, Bayern Munich employed an aggressive, man-marking high press. This tactical approach faced heavy criticism, primarily due to the potential for conceding counterattack goals. Despite the fact that several clubs, such as Atalanta Bergamo, had already been successfully using man-marking in high pressing for years on the international stage, the approach was viewed as atypical in Germany. Since the 1990s, man-marking had largely been replaced in the Bundesliga by zonal marking or hybrid forms. The evaluation of Bayern’s pressing was guided by historical prototypes of man-marking, particularly those involving a libero and, thus, a structural numerical inferiority. Although the man-marking was implemented in a completely different tactical fashion, the comparison seemed plausible due to the similarity and influenced judgments about its success.

    In reality, the base rates painted a different picture: Bayern dominated their early Bundesliga matches, prevented opponents from gaining a foothold, and significantly limited their scoring opportunities. Statistically, the approach was highly successful: in their first 11 matches, 7 opponents failed to exceed an xG value of 0.5. The previous season’s champions, Leverkusen, only managed an xG of 0.17 and just 27% possession.

    Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, the assessment of Bayern’s man-marking pressing was distorted by the representativeness heuristic: instead of evaluating the actual likelihood of success based on objective data, the plausibility of an outdated playing style was used as the basis of judgment. This illustrates how stereotypical mental models can lead to misjudgments and how crucial it is to critically examine information in football analysis.

    For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that individual statistics (base rates in football) are not necessarily meaningful on their own. However, a combination of multiple statistics and data points can produce a more reliable picture to guide analysis. While xG values (as a combination of several data inputs) are still prone to error and need to be contextualized, they can nonetheless provide valuable insights into a team’s actual performance over time.

    The conjunction fallacy is one of the cognitive errors that arise from the representativeness heuristic. It describes the tendency of people to judge the combination of two events as more likely than one of the events alone, even when directly compared. The prerequisite is that the combination creates a more coherent and plausible story than the single event. One of the most controversial and well-known examples is the “Linda problem” by Kahneman and Tversky:.

    According to recent reports, “Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

    Which of the following is more probable?

    Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.”.

    Sources indicate that despite the intuitive plausibility that Linda’s characteristics align more closely with the feminist movement, the first option is statistically more probable. After all, the conjunction of two events (“Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement”) is always less likely than one of the events alone (“Linda is a bank teller”).

    In a recent development, „The most representative outcomes combine with the personality description to yield the most coherent stories. The most coherent stories are not necessarily the most probable, but they are plausible, and the concepts of coherence, plausibility, and probability are easily confused by the unwary.“ – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    The “less-is-more pattern” by Christopher Hsee ties into this problem. For those who want to read more, I’ve linked the relevant study here. It states that the probability of the broader event (e.g., Linda is a bank teller) must be higher than that of the event that is included within it (e.g., Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement). However, the more plausible event (less comprehensive) is judged to be more probable than the less plausible, more comprehensive one. This creates the “less-is-more” pattern. As a result, the probability estimate for the more detailed scenario is higher, even though this contradicts logical reasoning.

    “This is the trap for forecasters and their clients: the more detailed the scenarios, the more convincing they are, but the less probable they become.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Industry observers note that in the context of opponent team analysis for an upcoming match, the analyst must be aware that they are the forecaster, making probability estimates about the opponent’s future style of play. Thus, they should assess the likelihood of events, not merely their plausibility.

    It has been revealed that applying Hsee’s “less-is-more principle” to this context means that detailed, plausible match scenarios may sound impressive, but are statistically less reliable for prediction than broader descriptions. Each additional assumption in a forecast multiplies individual probabilities and thereby reduces the overall likelihood of an accurate prediction.

    According to recent reports, however, this is not a call for a lack of detail in opponent analysis. On the contrary, the more detailed, precise, and comprehensive the analysis, the better the ability to derive general playing principles, patterns, and behaviors of the opponent. Therefore, the analyst should aim to analyze the opponent as holistically as possible before making generalized statements that increase the predictive probability.

    While in Part 2 I will address structural conditions in football that affect the intuition of analyst and coach experts, in this section I will focus on the individual conditions of different types of analysis. Even though I speak here about football analysis in general, it is notable to clarify that there are various forms of analysis in football (see table). Different types of analysis also have different individual susceptibilities to cognitive biases.

    It has been revealed that certain biases are additionally triggered by specific types of analysis. Prediction, for example, is particularly affected by the representativeness heuristic, since it involves assessing probabilities. Team analysis over multiple games increases susceptibility to the anchoring heuristic, and post-match analysis is prone to hindsight bias, the tendency to overestimate the predictability of an event after it has occurred.

    Industry observers note that similarly, focusing on a single level of analysis increases vulnerability to WYSIATI. You should now be familiar with the cognitive errors mentioned here, so they should not come as a surprise. One factor not yet addressed in this article, which demonstrably increases susceptibility to all biases, is time pressure. Time pressure plays a significant role especially during live analysis, though not exclusively.

    Industry observers note that time pressure forces analysts to make quicker decisions. Research reveals that under such conditions, people rely more heavily on heuristics, increasing the likelihood of errors. Among other studies, Finucane et al. (2000) examined the influence of the affect heuristic on the evaluation of benefits and risks, demonstrating that time pressure amplifies this effect.

    Analysts therefore have to rely more on their intuition during live analysis. This brings me to Part 2, where I will identify conditions that increase experts’ susceptibility to intuitive errors.

    By now, it should be clear why we delve so deeply into the mechanisms of heuristics. Without a fundamental understanding of how they work, heuristics and cognitive biases are difficult to recognize.

    Many behavioral psychology insights can be profitably applied in sports analysis. This includes not only heuristics and cognitive biases but can also be extended to other areas of football analysis. However, to cover these application areas sufficiently, there will be a Part 2, Part 3, and, if necessary, a Part 4.

    In Part 2, I will address the topic of overconfidence. Among other things, it will examine the susceptibility of expert intuition as well as risk strategies and risk assessments in football. Strategies for avoiding biases in football analysis will also be presented.

    Part 3 (and possibly Part 4) will focus on “noise” in football analysis. Unlike bias, noise does not describe the distortion of judgments in a particular direction but the unconscious variability of multiple judgments under identical decision conditions.

    In a recent development, author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

    CBS Sports ranked Gray as the No. 14 free agent available on the market this offseason. Here's our write-up:.

He completed six innings 22 times in his 29 starts this past season, which makes him a workhorse by 2026 standards. Gray will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 37 and he's lost enough velocity to shrink his margin of error meaningfully, which creates some over-the-cliff risk. Still, the 14-year veteran is not out of place as the No. 2 starter in a postseason rotation.

    Industry observers note that gray now joins a Twins rotation that includes Taj Bradley, Joe Ryan and Pablo López, who missed last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery in February. Other options include Dean Kremer, Bailey Ober and Mick Abel.

That landed them in third place in the American League Central and seven games out of the third and final wild-card spot in the AL. Although the Twins improved upon their 2025 record, they've now missed the postseason for three straight years, their longest drought in a decade. The Gray addition -- plus catcher Ryan Jeffers' acceptance of the qualifying offer for 2027 -- helps the cause, and no doubt the Twins under second-year manager Derek Shelton will be looking to get back to the playoffs in what again figures to be a winnable division.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, it's time to call off the search, Ponce de León, the San Francisco 49ers have struck gold once again.
    • Recent findings suggest that sometimes all we can do is turn to an old legend to explain how a bunch of geriatrics subdued Father Time and a substation (theory) up to this point.
    • Industry observers note that as the 49ers prepare for one of the biggest games of the year vs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, it's time to call off the search, Ponce de León, the San Francisco 49ers have struck gold once again. They've found the Fountain of Youth.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes all we can do is turn to an old legend to explain how a bunch of geriatrics subdued Father Time and a substation (theory) up to this point. They've raced out to an 8-1 start despite having the oldest (28.4 average age) and most injured (19.7 player games missed due to injury per game) team in the National Football League.

    Industry observers note that as the 49ers prepare for one of the biggest games of the year vs. the Vikings in Mexico City on Sunday (between scheme gods Kyle Shanahan and Brian Flores), I'm marveling at just how incredible they've been at the midway point.

    Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy are in their bag, and Christian McCaffrey is still one of the league's best weapons at age 30, even after a season with 450 touches.

    George Kittle is cooking at age 33, less than a year removed from a torn Achilles. Trent Williams (age 38) is still trucking upfield, leading convoys. Purdy-to-Mike-Evans (age 33) was the league's best combo until Evans got hurt. Deebo Samuel (age 30) has even turned back the clock.

    Nobody is using the peanut punch like Fred Warner, who just turned 30 on Thursday. Nick Bosa (age 29) is working his way back into form after his calf injury (and last year's torn ACL). It won't be long before trade deadline acquisitions Keenan Allen (34) and DeForest Buckner (32) get in on the act, too.

    It's incredible when you consider the injury history of some of those guys. I'm just going to assume doctors replaced some of those broken bones and torn ligaments with some 'Terminator' stuff because they are straight-up bots.

    Recent findings suggest that the old guard has stunningly remained intact up to this point. The same can't be noted about the rest of the team. The 49ers' entire WR core and defensive line have been wiped out. At one point, the 49ers' top six wideouts entering the year were out: Mike Evans, Ricky Pearsall, De'Zhaun Stribling, Deebo Samuel, Christian Kirk and Demarcus Robinson.

    It has been revealed that injuries ravaged the d-line with Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, Alfred Collins, C.J. West and Gracen Halton out at different times. Kyle Juszczyk, Mike Evans and Dre Greenlaw have notably missed action as well.

    It's not shocking to see the 49ers playing well, especially given how they persevered last year, but they are taking it to a completely different level this season.

    This is the most decorated offense on paper in NFL history. The 49ers have the most combined Pro Bowl selections (48) on offense by any team in NFL history. It's an embarrassment of riches, but it doesn't always translate. San Francisco is certainly cashing in, though, with one of the most efficient offenses in modern history.

    They have the highest success rate (55.2%) of any offense in a season this century. Meaning, they keep their offense on schedule, ahead of the chains, better than any unit ever recorded. Overall, they have the most efficient unit, in terms of EPA per play (0.19), since the 2018 Chiefs, when Patrick Mahomes threw for 50 touchdown passes. San Francisco is scoring touchdowns at the third-highest rate (39% of drives) since 2000, behind the 2007 Patriots (who went 16-0 with MVP Tom Brady tossing 50 touchdowns) and the 2020 Packers (with MVP Aaron Rodgers, who had 48 touchdowns and five interceptions).

    Brock Purdy has the highest EPA per dropback (0.34) since Lamar Jackson in 2019, his unanimous MVP year.

    Amazingly, they are in the company of legends despite having the oldest offense, weighted by playing time, since at least 2010 (30.0).

    Industry observers note that and the most stunning part is how they are doing it. It's crazy to see their old core look like they are still in their primes. Deebo Samuel was clocked at his fastest speed in two years (20.39 MPH) when he took this hook-and-ladder 80 yards to the house. He made another house call at 19.96 MPH in Dallas last week.

    HOOK-AND-LADDER TD 🤯Deebo Samuel traveled a total distance of 110.35 yards and reached a max speed of 20.39 MPH on this 80-yard touchdown, per @NextGenStats @AZvsSF on FOX/FOX OneStream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/88dsZtSZum.

    In a recent development, christian McCaffrey turned Jerry World into a track meet with a 66-yard TD reception to ice the game, where he was clocked at 20.29 MPH. That was his fastest speed in over three years and faster than any Jahmyr Gibbs play this year.

    Sources indicate that christian McCaffrey reached 20.29 MPH on this play. That's his fourth-fastest speed since joining the 49ers and his top speed in a game since Week 14 of 2023. pic.twitter.com/TJnSOYzRw3.

    Perhaps the most shocking was George Kittle getting clocked at his fastest speed in seven years earlier this season vs. Denver, nine months removed from his Achilles injury.

    George Kittle reached 19.84 mph on this play, per Next Gen Stats. That's the same speed as Xavier Worthy's 41-yard TD today. It doesn't make sense for a player fresh off an Achilles injury to hit these kinda speeds so soon.He's a freak. pic.twitter.com/NPYVdpKeaD.

    See what I'm saying?! They have literally found the Fountain of Youth. They account for five of the longest touchdowns by 30+ year olds this year. Last week, they became the first team ever with three 50-yard scores in a game from 30+ year olds and the first team, regardless of age, with three 65-yard scores since the 2000 "greatest show on turf" Rams.

    Longest TD Scored by Age 30+ players this yearDeebo Samuel 80 yards (49ers)Christian McCaffrey 74 yards (49ers)Deebo Samuel 70 yards (49ers)Christian McCaffrey 66 yards (49ers)George Kittle 56 yards (49ers).

    Sources indicate that they are going to obliterate old man records. The 49ers have 30 touchdowns from 30+ year olds this season, putting them on pace for 56! The record is 36 by the 1994 49ers and 2002 Raiders.

    They are on pace for 5,028 scrimmage yards from 30-somethings. The only team with 4,000 was the 2002 Raiders (5,016), who were anchored by Jerry Rice and Tim Brown.

    The 49ers are responsible for 22% of the league's touchdowns from 30-plus year olds, and no other team has more than 13.

    Recent findings suggest that they have 555 yards worth of touchdowns from 30-plus-year-olds. No other team has cracked 500 this year, from all players! It's just silly.

    If you weighted their age by scrimmage yards only, the only squad in league history older than this 49ers team is the aforementioned early-2000s Raiders.

    Recent findings suggest that it goes beyond age and scoring. I can confidently say we have never seen a team quite like the 49ers, at least in modern times.

    As mentioned off the top, the 49ers are the oldest and most injured team in the league this year.

    I looked at every team since 2010, using data from SportRadar, to dive a little deeper.

    That's 544 team seasons in that span. The 2026 49ers have the sixth-most games missed due to injury (19.7 per game) and the third-oldest (28.4) roster among those 544 teams. That is why, in the illustration below comparing age and injuries, the 49ers are light years away from all other teams in that span.

    They are the only team of the 544 to rank top among the top three in a season in each of the following: Win percentage, oldest team, and most injured team.

    Those numbers are madness. They defy logic, right? Teams aren't supposed to be this good when they are this old and injured. So can they sustain it and win their first Super Bowl since the 1994 season?

    General manager John Lynch addressed the age concerns last week on KNBR's morning show, "Murph & Markus".

    According to recent reports, "I don't think that's a conscious thing. We're not saying, 'Let's go find every old guy.' I've talked about it a lot, and we really feel [this]," Lynch noted. "We think it's a good mix because we have those vets, and it's skewed a little bit. Our long snapper [Jon Weeks] is 40 years old. I don't worry about that. He snaps the football and that's tough to do, and he does it very well. Weeks, Trent Williams, I'll take that. [Williams] defies age and the things. I do think there's some level of, 35 is the new 30.

    According to recent reports, "These guys are taking such great care of themselves, but I feel really good that we've insulated ourselves with that core group, but then we've got a lot of young contributors. You saw [linebacker Jaden Dugger] with the pick-six, Romello Height, god bless Gracen Halton because that was tough to see him going out. Upton Stout, Renardo Green are young players. We've got young players all over playing integral roles. I think it's a really good mix.".

    Recent findings suggest that here's the blueprint they are trying to follow. It's the 1998 Broncos with John Elway, Michael Jordan's "Last Dance" with the 1998 Bulls, and the 2001 Diamondbacks with old horses like Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. Those are the oldest teams in each respective sport to win titles in modern history.

    The Patriots had the oldest team in the league in 2018 when they won their last title with Tom Brady.

    Sources indicate that it's also been done before, by a Shanahan. The 49ers are the oldest team (28.4) to start 8-1 or better since the 1998 Broncos, coached by Kyle Shanahan's dad, Mike. Those Broncos are the only team older than these 49ers to win a Super Bowl.

    So age is not the problem. Old teams can win, and analysis of those 544 seasons since 2010 indicates there's even a slight correlation between older teams and more winning.

    It has been revealed that the key then is the 49ers' health, specifically their aging studs. They've proven they can produce like Hall of Famers in their prime, but can they stay on the field in January and February?

    Industry observers note that this team is traveling 38,105 miles and crossing 58 time zones (both shattering NFL records) over 17 regular season games. Home-field advantage would be massive for them. Either way, 20 to 21 games when you include playoffs is quite the toll, especially when they are playing in one of the toughest divisions in football and still have games left vs. the Vikings, Seahawks, Giants, Rams and Chiefs.

    The 1998 Broncos team had seven Pro Bowlers in their thirties, the most by any team since 1970. None of those seven (John Elway, Ed McCaffrey, Shannon Sharpe, Mark Schlereth, Tony Jones, Bill Romanowski, Steve Atwater) missed a playoff game.

    In a recent development, the stars would need to align for San Francisco, too. Up to this point, their core of Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Mike Evans, Trent Williams, Nick Bosa, and Fred Warner have combined to miss just eight games this year (three by Evans, five by Bosa).

    How can we trust the 49ers' track record here?

    According to recent reports, last year, their top six highest-paid players missed 64 games. The year prior, they were ravaged by the most significant injuries to star players the league has ever seen.

    Let's drop Evans from the equation because this is his first year with the 49ers. The other six (Purdy, McCaffrey, Kittle, Williams, Bosa, Warner) have all played in 43% of the 49ers games since Purdy made his first career start in 2022. San Francisco is 27-4 in those games and 21-21 in all other games, including playoffs.

    Recent findings suggest that they haven't lost with all six playing since the Super Bowl vs. the Chiefs.

    In a recent development, so if the 49ers core doesn't stay healthy for an entire playoff run, they can kiss a championship goodbye. And the likelihood of them staying on the field seems slim.

    According to recent reports, however, they've already done something nearly impossible by finding the Fountain of Youth, so we can't discount another miracle. Maybe they will capture the holy grail too, a Super Bowl.

    #50196. Ranking the NBA's most hopeless teams: Which franchise is in the bleakest situation? And who can't fix it?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2137 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Ranking the NBA's most hopeless teams: Which franchise is in the bleakest situation? And who can't fix it?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well.
    • Sources indicate that the question here is how bleak.
    • According to recent reports, to be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well. Though the final score showed only a seven-point margin, the Miami Heat led by 26 after three quarters and were never in much danger. The defeat dropped the Bucks to 1-14 on the season. The greatest player in their franchise's history now wears another jersey, and they're at the beginning of what figures to be a very long rebuild. Things are bleak.

    Sources indicate that the question here is how bleak. Milwaukee knew it would spend this season in the cellar. It probably expects to live there for a few years. But how far away from winning seriously are the Bucks really? Are they further from genuine contention than any other team in the NBA? Who, right now, has the bleakest long-term outlook?

    According to recent reports, to be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity. We don't care if you have a chance to be a plucky .500 team. No, the barometer we're using here is how likely each team is to reach a conference finals in the next five seasons. We're accounting not only for players on the existing roster, but long-term financial flexibility, available draft assets and the competence of the front office helming these organizations. With all of that in mind, let's rank the NBA's most hopeless long-term outlooks.

    The broad sentiment following their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard was that the Clippers faced the bleakest future in the entire NBA. That's probably overstating things slightly.

    It has been revealed that remember, we're talking about a Los Angeles team here. Someone, inevitably, is going to want to play for them. All it takes is one player bucking the league-wide trend against superstar free agency and they're back in business. They have an owner who will spare no expense in pursuit of wins, and there's a 26-year-old All-Star in Darius Garland already on the roster. Couple that with the hope generated by No. 5 overall pick Keaton Wagler, and while the path here is extremely narrow, it exists. If the Brooklyn Nets could build a contender without draft picks in the late 2010s, it's theoretically possible for the Clippers to do the same.

    Of course, the Nets weren't subject to that league-wide pivot away from free agency. They didn't have to trade picks to get Kevin Durant or Kyrie Irving in the door. It's much, much harder nowadays to import talent like that without sacrificing picks that the Clippers frankly don't have. The five first-round picks they were docked in the Leonard investigation left them fully Stepien-locked: while they will have (not especially valuable) first-round picks in odd-numbered years moving forward, they can't trade any of them yet.

    There's also the reputational hit the Clippers just took. Will players interested in winning want to risk their careers on a team that cheated? Can the Clippers even appeal to such players given their asset deficit? These are going to be real hurdles. Their path to the conference finals might rely on a star who's not especially competitive. After all, anyone serious about winning could find a team closer to doing so.

    In a recent development, they're a blank slate with one very promising prospect. Darius Acuff is putting up star box-score numbers in his rookie season. That's by no means a guarantee of future stardom, of course. He's as inefficient as you'd expect a rookie to be on this volume. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey or Dwyane Wade ever did over a full season. But Acuff has a path to becoming one of the NBA's best offensive point guards. These aren't totally empty calories.

    In a recent development, there's nothing else here. No other notable prospects aside from a handful of likely long-term bench youngsters (Dylan Cardwell, Maxime Raynaud, Emanuel Sharp). Sacramento mostly controls its own picks (aside from the 2031 swap it inexplicably gave San Antonio in the DeMar DeRozan sign-and-trade), but that means less than it used to in the lottery reform era. Its books slowly clean up in the offseasons to come, with Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter expiring after this season and Domantas Sabonis and Malik Monk joining them in the summer of 2028, but Sacramento's forays into cap space have typically been unsuccessful. This isn't exactly a desirable destination. That's what happens when you miss the playoffs 19 times in 20 years.

    That's what separates Sacramento from fellow "one possible star, otherwise blank slate" candidates like the Chicago Bulls. With the hire of Bryson Graham to run basketball operations, the Bulls at least appear to be trending towards becoming a normal organization. Normalcy has eternally eluded Sacramento. The burden of proof is on the Kings. When you've been a mess for 20 years, it's on you to prove that you've cleaned up your act. We'll trust the Kings when they've earned it and not a second sooner.

    For now, they can at least start by actually keeping their success stories in the building. They've kept only one first-round pick this decade through the end of his rookie contract: Keegan Murray, who is now pretty substantially overpaid. Meanwhile, Tyrese Haliburton has blossomed into a superstar in Indiana, while their entire 2021 draft class (Davion Mitchell and Neemias Queta) now starts for Eastern Conference championship hopefuls. They had the unanimous Coach of the Year and the Executive of the Year and fired both within two years. The Kings can't help themselves.

    There's far more talent in the cupboard here than in Sacramento, but the same organizational concerns apply. The Joe Dumars regime makes mistakes -- the two-year minimum for DeAndre Jordan, not waiting until after the 2025 Finals to trade Indiana its 2026 pick back, everything Shamit Dua has reported about the infamous Derik Queen trade -- that typical teams would never dream of.

    There is not a discernible proposal here besides, seemingly, "acquire players who can put the ball through the hoop." There are a lot of decent individual creators on this roster. None of them synergize well because so few of them can consistently make 3s and all of them are on-ball players with stylistic clashes. The Pelicans have seemingly made the determination, for instance, that Queen cannot play significant minutes alongside Zion Williamson. That's a reasonable choice... but then why is Williamson still on the team? Or, if the Pelicans view him as a fixture, why make such a risky trade for Queen in the first place?

    Industry observers note that the trickle-down effect of putting all of these dribblers on the same team is that none of them seem happy to be on it. Dejounte Murray asked for a trade. Jordan Poole is making googly eyes at the Warriors. Trey Murphy has reportedly signaled a desire to move. What is the plan here? What kind of team are the Pelicans trying to build? What do they view as their path to genuine winning?

    Recent findings suggest that that's what distinguishes New Orleans from Sacramento. If the Kings get a few more high draft picks and use them on players that complement Acuff, I'd see the vision. It would require Acuff becoming an All-NBA scorer and those picks hitting, but I see the sort of teams they could build, even if they're unlikely to actually do so. I have no earthly idea what the Pelicans would do with a few high picks because talent is not currently the problem. It's how they're using and nurturing it. It's just hard to envision a team with so little understanding of how to balance skill sets and bring out the best in their players making a serious playoff push. Something significant in the organization would have to change.

    They're the best team on this list in the present, and they've clawed their way back to .500 after a miserable start that included leaks about the team's lack of a point guard. Again, we're dealing in upside here. That's what the Suns lack.

    It has been revealed that they control none of their own first-round picks in the seven-year tradable window except for their 2032 selection... which is frozen because they spent the 2024-25 season above the second apron. Even if they had picks, the Suns under Matt Ishbia have never displayed any discipline in using them. Ishbia traded nearly a full draft for Kevin Durant mere days after acquiring the team, spent an unprotected 2031 pick on three far lesser choices that amounted to Mark Williams and a Jusuf Nurkić cap dump, and then spent their 2033 pick as soon as they could access it to get Miles Bridges, whom they've been meaningfully better without thus far this season.

    The most talented players here are all right around their physical peaks. Devin Booker is 30. Dillon Brooks turns 31 this season, and Bridges turns 29. They're going to get worse, not better, and without draft picks, their means of replacing them are minimal. Even the diamonds they've dug out of the rough are on the older side. Collin Gillespie is 27. Jordan Goodwin is 28. The truly young players, like Khaman Maluach and Rasheer Fleming, have thus far underwhelmed. The younger, star-level talent here is Jalen Green, who plays Booker's position and has been a disaster on both ends this season. Why exactly is he still starting over Gillespie? Are the Suns just trying to salvage his trade value?

    Teams like the Clippers, Kings and Pelicans are at least young enough and financially flexible enough to grow. The Suns, at least from an asset and financial standpoint, are essentially all-in on a Play-In-caliber roster. That Play-In-caliber roster is going to get worse as it gets older and more expensive and, without access to top talent in the draft, replenishing it is going to be borderline impossible.

    Industry observers note that the Bucks cherry-pick traits from all of our other selections. The Clippers circumvented the cap; the Bucks are getting investigated for doing so with Gary Trent Jr. The Pelicans have a roster full of overlapping skill sets; the Bucks have a million shooting guards, which made the decision to re-sign Trent for $64 million all the stranger. The Suns don't control any of their own picks and the Bucks won't until 2031 at the earliest. The Kings have the NBA's least-successful owner in Vivek Ranadivé, while the Bucks may have the NFL's in Jimmy Haslam, though he technically won't become governor until 2028 due to Milwaukee's bizarre ownership structure (another point against them, as successful teams tend to have stable leadership rather than rotating five-year terms).

    Industry observers note that who is going to be the best player on the team in five years? Brayden Burries is the best long-term prospect, but he profiles as more of a high-end role player. Tyler Herro was an All-Star in the sense that Norman Powell and D'Angelo Russell were All-Stars: they put up massive numbers in a weak Eastern Conference. Kel'El Ware was the lottery ticket from the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade and he's been so bad that he's somehow playing less than he did on a Heat team that was trying to win. Without access to their own picks or a market that tends to draw free agents, they're basically hoping someone internal (Nate Ament? Ryan Rollins?) breaks out or that they hit on a pick far later than you should rely on.

    You could argue that just by virtue of being in the Eastern Conference, the Bucks have a cleaner path to the final four than those West teams do because they don't have to worry about Victor Wembanyama or the specter of healthier versions of the Oklahoma City Thunder down the line. That's fair, but as we've seen this year, injuries loom over every season. You know what else the West has aside from those two juggernauts? The four other teams on this list. The Bucks, by a wide margin, are the most hopeless team in their own conference. They're starting from the absolute bottom.

    It has been revealed that this was potentially avoidable. Had they acted sooner and traded Antetokounmpo in 2025 when the whole world knew a deal was eventually coming, they could have secured a stronger return and set themselves up for a quicker turnaround. Alas, the Bucks chose to waive-and-stretch Damian Lillard, locking them into $22.5 million in dead money through the end of the decade so they could sign Myles Turner to a contract that is increasingly looking like $28 million or so per year in... close to dead money. Milwaukee got its championship in 2021, but at this rate, it's going to be a while before it sniffs another one.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday stated club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a upcoming collective bargaining agreement.
    • "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred noted while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.
    • Industry observers note that "Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred said later during a news conference at MLB headquarters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday stated club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a upcoming collective bargaining agreement. While Manfred noted there was general room for compromise with the MLBPA, that does not extend to the central matter of the capped system owners want.

    "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred noted while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.

    Industry observers note that "Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred said later during a news conference at MLB headquarters. "I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive.".

    It's possible to parse "can't imagine" as a subtle rhetorical hedge. Additionally, Manfred before he was commissioner was the league's lead negotiator. As such, he's quite familiar with the appearance of unyielding resolve as a tactical implement. Thus, the league has tied every other proposed change to the players' acceptance of a cap and floor, and the players through their union have historically shown zero willingness to accept such a system.

    "There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer said Wednesday in a statement.

    According to recent reports, "There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries.".

    In a recent development, in their most recent substantive proposal to the players, MLB pitched a $258.3 million cap and $180.2 million floor on team payrolls, with those limits to be phased in gradually. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor.

    It has been revealed that the current CBA, which is the accord that governs every aspect of the working relationship between players and clubs in MLB, is set to expire just before midnight on Dec. 1. At that point, the league is expected to lock out the players at the behest of team owners. The lockout will likely not end until a upcoming CBA is agreed to, at least in principle. Owners also locked out the players in 2021, and that lockout lasted 99 days and very nearly ate into the 2022 regular-season schedule.
